# 044 · A constant-pool encoder that writes NUL as one byte emits the byte no class file may hold

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional, compatibility | high | bug-fix, behaviour change not intended | [`ModifiedUtf8#firstByte`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/classfile/ModifiedUtf8.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../lib/README.md) |

> The class-file writer encodes `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` in modified UTF-8, where U+0000 takes two bytes so that no byte of an encoded string is zero. A developer aligns the encoder with standard UTF-8, one byte for every character up to U+007F, and updates the test that said otherwise. The property the build proves of the encoder, that no first byte is zero, is refuted on the one input it can be: the character U+0000, encoded as the byte 0, which JVMS §4.4.7 says no `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` may contain.

Tags: [jvm-internals](../README.md#tag-jvm-internals), [class-files](../README.md#tag-class-files), [text-encoding](../README.md#tag-text-encoding)

## The change

Encode a character up to U+007F as one byte, U+0000 included, in the length, the first byte and the encoder: the two-byte form for NUL is not UTF-8, and tools that read the constant pool with a standard decoder see `C0 80` as an invalid sequence. The tests `nulTakesTwoBytes` and `nulAndTheHigherPlanesAreEncodedAsTheSpecificationSays` are renamed and their expectations changed; the string-length test is adjusted by one. All tests pass.

**Before** ([`ModifiedUtf8.java`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/classfile/ModifiedUtf8.java), line 1):

 * two-byte form and supplementary characters are encoded as their two surrogates, three bytes each. The two
 * exceptions have one purpose: no byte of an encoded string is zero, so that the virtual machine can hand the

 * {@code ClassFormatError}.
 */

        }
        return c <= 0x07ff ? 2 : 3;

            return c;
        }
        if (c <= 0x07ff) {
    // ...

        int k = 0;
        for (char c : chars) {
            if (c >= 0x0001 && c <= 0x007f) {
                out[k++] = (byte) c;
            } else if (c <= 0x07ff) {
                out[k++] = (byte) (0xc0 | (c >> 6));

## What the verifier found

The property `result != 0 && result <= 255 && ((result >= 192) == (c == 0 || c >= 128))` does not hold on every input. The prover found this input, and the tool replayed it on the method to show what it does:

| Input | The method's outcome |
|---|---|
| `firstByte(c='\u0000')` | `0` |

One input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `c: char`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

A class file with a zero byte inside a `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` is rejected by every conforming class loader with a `ClassFormatError`, HotSpot's included: the specification says no byte may be zero, and HotSpot checks it when it parses the constant pool. A string constant with an embedded NUL (a C-style terminator in a protocol, a padding character, a `\0` in a test fixture) now produces a class the virtual machine will not load, from source that compiled fine. The two-byte NUL is the reason modified UTF-8 exists: the runtime hands the bytes of a symbol to C code as a string, and counts its length without decoding, both of which a zero byte would end early. The developer read the encoding as a bug in the encoder, and the test that said otherwise as a bug in the test.

## Why the verdict is right

The property committed for `firstByte` states the invariant the format is built on: the first byte is never zero, is at most 255, and is a multi-byte lead exactly for U+0000 and for characters from U+0080 up. JBMC turns the harness into a satisfiability problem over every `char`, and the only one that fails it is U+0000, whose first byte is now 0; the tool replays it in its interpreter and shows the outcome. The witness is the one the specification names, and the property as committed is the sentence of §4.4.7 that the change contradicts.

## What to do

Revert, including the test. If a reader with a standard UTF-8 decoder is the problem, the reader is wrong for class files: it has to decode modified UTF-8, as `DataInputStream.readUTF` does, and so has the class-file API of the JDK. The property stays as the regression test for the next person who takes the two-byte NUL for a bug.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: found by JBMC 6.11.0 in 0.1 s searching inputs in [0:20], replayed in the interpreter; domain c: char.

This result was recorded before runs fingerprinted their inputs, so whether it still matches the current patch and sources is not known.
